note: The Lexicon of the Journey. DRAFT, written for this piece, for review by teachers of the Royal Ballet School and the Centre for Dance Studies. Descriptions are original; dates and places are approximate where the history is uncertain. Fields: t term; gr Greek; lit literal meaning; does what is danced; fam family; place, lat, lon, year of origin; schools differences between schools; status shared (every school, what remains) | living | rare | historical | lost; home athens|london (a tie to one of the homes); move the meadow's motion.

terms.lit: dance; a band who dance and sing
terms.does: In ancient Greece a group of dancers and singers moving together, and the dance itself. The root of chorus and choreography.
The dignified, measured dance of Greek tragedy.
The bawdy, energetic dance of Old Comedy.
The leaping, mocking dance of the satyr play.
An armed dance imitating attack and defence, taught to the young; danced in Sparta and Athens.
A winding chain dance said to retrace the paths of the Labyrinth, danced on Delos in memory of Theseus.
A lively song accompanied by mimetic dance.
Expressive movement of hands and arms; a distant ancestor of port de bras.
The Greek word for the art of dance, praised by Plato and, much later, Lucian.
Order in movement. For Plato, the sense the gods gave us that lets humans dance.
A line dance of gliding steps, the dancers joined by the hands; the leader improvises.
A festive circle dance in 7/8, twelve steps to a phrase.
A line dance, hands on shoulders, from the butchers' guild of Constantinople.
A solo in 9/8, improvised, turning in on itself; by custom never applauded.
A proud dance of high leaps and turns by the first dancer, the line holding him.
A fast Cretan war dance, shoulders linked, gathering speed.
In fifteenth-century Italian treatises, the proportion between music and step.
A slow processional court dance of gliding steps kept close to the ground.

terms.lit: of Padua, or of the peacock
terms.does: A stately procession of couples.
A vigorous after-dance of hops and kicks on five steps, the cinq pas.
A couple dance in which the man lifts the woman high as they turn.
A chain dance of side steps, the commonest dance of court and village alike.
Thoinot Arbeau's 1589 manual, written as a dialogue, recording the dances of his day.
The five placements of the feet, turned out from the hip, from which every step begins and ends. Codified by Pierre Beauchamp.
Turned out; and turning away from the supporting leg.
Turning toward the supporting leg.
A bending of the knees, smooth and continuous: demi, half; grand, full. The first exercise of every class.
A rise onto half-pointe or pointe.
The working foot slides out until only the toes touch the floor, then returns.
A tendu that leaves the floor a little, quick and sharp.
terms.schools: The Russian school calls it battement tendu jeté; the Cecchetti school and the RAD, battement glissé or dégagé.

terms.does: The leg draws a half circle, on the floor or in the air.
From the ankle the foot strikes outward sharply to full extension.
A slow sinking on the supporting leg while the other unfolds.
A movement of the working leg out and back; grand battement throws it high.
The leg draws up to the knee, then unfolds into the air.
The arms moving through their positions; also a whole exercise of arms and body.
The angle of the shoulders and head against the hips, giving a step its light and shade.
terms.schools: Most strongly emphasised in the Russian and English schools.

terms.does: One foot chases the other out of its place in a gliding step.
A travelling step that glides from fifth position to fifth.
Three small quick steps, from the old folk dance of the Auvergne.
One foot cuts the other away; a quick transfer of weight.
A jump from one foot to the other, the working leg thrown out.
A jump from one foot landing on two, the legs brought together in the air.

terms.lit: named, it is said, after the Comte de Sissonne
terms.does: A jump from two feet to one, the legs opening like scissors.
In the air, the lower leg beats up against the raised one.
A straight jump in which the legs cross and beat in the air, counted by crossings.
A complete turn on one leg, on pointe or half-pointe.
A waltzing step, down-up-down in three counts.
A swinging step in three from the folk dances of the Basque country.
The courtly dance in three, of small steps and bows, danced at Versailles.
A slow, grave dance in three, once thought scandalous.

terms.lit: of the Gavots, the mountain people
terms.does: A moderate dance in two with small springing steps.
A gliding, running court dance; said to be Louis XIV's favourite.
The bow at the end of class, thanking teacher and pianist.
Raoul-Auger Feuillet's 1700 notation of steps as signs on the page; later, the making of dances.
Slow sustained movement showing balance and line; in the pas de deux, the slow first part.
Bright fast steps and jumps: petit allegro small, grand allegro high and travelling.
The look of floating in a jump, landing as softly as rising.
The height a dancer reaches in a jump.
A hop on one foot.
terms.schools: The RAD and the Cecchetti school say temps levé for a hop and sauté for a jump on two feet; usage varies elsewhere.

terms.does: A jump, usually from two feet to two.
A jump in fifth position, changing feet in the air.
Both feet escape from fifth to second position, jumped or on pointe.
A light sideways jump, each leg drawn up in turn.
terms.schools: The Russian version often throws the second leg out backward; the English and French keep both legs bent.

terms.does: A dance for two; the classical form runs entrée, adagio, two variations and coda.
A suite of dances that pauses the story to show the dancers.
The body on one leg, the other extended long behind, the arms prolonging the line.
terms.schools: Vaganova numbers four arabesques, Cecchetti five, the RAD three.

terms.does: Like an arabesque, the raised leg bent at the knee. Carlo Blasis said he took it from Giambologna's Mercury.
Dancing on the tips of the toes. Marie Taglioni made it poetry in La Sylphide, Paris, 1832.
Tiny even steps on pointe that seem to float across the stage.

terms.lit: a nursery word of uncertain origin
terms.does: The ballerina's skirt: long and romantic in the 1830s, short and stiff by the 1880s.
The moonlit acts of spirits, wilis and swans, danced in white.
Steps joined into a phrase. In the Bournonville school, set classes for each day of the week.
A turn driven by the leg whipping out and in. Pierina Legnani first danced thirty-two in a row, St Petersburg, 1893.
Turns or leaps travelling in a circle around the stage.
Stepping directly onto a straight leg on pointe or half-pointe.
Quick turns on both feet, travelling in a line.
A jump straight up with one or two full turns.
Fixed daily exercises for each day of the week; his London school from 1918 shaped English teaching.
Petipa's grand ensemble showpiece of soloists and corps.
A solo within a larger work.
The fast closing section of a pas de deux or grand pas.
The ensemble, dancing as one.
Her system, published in Leningrad in 1934, joining French grace, Italian strength and Russian expressiveness.
A leap that turns in the air.
terms.schools: Grand jeté en tournant in the Cecchetti school and the RAD; jeté entrelacé in the Russian; tour jeté in America.

terms.does: The rail at which every class begins.
The part of class away from the barre, in the middle of the room.
The lyrical, precise manner of Frederick Ashton and the Royal Ballet: quick feet, épaulement, restraint.

terms.lit: the notation of Rudolf and Joan Benesh
terms.does: Movement written on a five-line stave, devised in London in 1955; the Royal Ballet's record of its repertory.
A system of symbols for movement, published in 1928.
Laban's eight qualities of movement: float, punch, glide, slash, dab, wring, press, flick.
Isadora Duncan's barefoot dance after Greek vases; she began a house on Kopanas hill near Athens in 1903.
The ancient chorus revived at the Delphic Festivals of 1927 and 1930, danced by Koula Pratsika's students.
German expressionist dance, Mary Wigman's above all, Dresden, 1920s.
Martha Graham's curving of the spine from the pelvis on the outbreath.
The letting go that answers a contraction; later, a family of techniques of weight and breath.
Doris Humphrey's arc between losing and regaining balance.
A twist of the torso around the spine, in Graham and much contemporary dance.
Merce Cunningham ordering movement by dice and the I Ching, freeing dance from story and music.
Dancers sharing weight through a moving point of contact; begun by Steve Paxton in 1972.
Pina Bausch's theatre of repetition, memory and everyday gesture, Wuppertal, from 1973.
William Forsythe's lines, points and planes for inventing movement, Frankfurt, 1990s.
Ohad Naharin's movement language of sensation and image, Tel Aviv.

chain: the dancing place of the theatre, from ορχούμαι, to dance
the players, no longer the floor
a band who dance and sing
the dancing is lost, the singing remains
Plato's school in Athens, a grove named for the hero Akademos
the Académie royale de danse, Paris, 1661
the Royal Academy of Dance, London, 1920
delight in dancing; the Muse of dance
